title: Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP)
passages: The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP) is a Medicare value-based purchasing program that links hospital payment to quality of care. It encourages hospitals to improve discharge planning and care coordination so patients and caregivers are more involved in their discharge plans.

Section 1886(q) of the Social Security Act required CMS to reduce payments to hospitals with excess readmissions starting fiscal year 2013. The 21st Century Cures Act added peer-group comparisons starting in fiscal year 2019.
HRRP tracks 30-day risk-standardized unplanned readmissions, focusing specifically on readmissions that could plausibly have been avoided with better post-discharge care.
HRRP measures currently cover acute myocardial infarction, COPD, heart failure, pneumonia, coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, and elective primary total hip and/or total knee arthroplasty.

Payment reductions under HRRP apply to Medicare fee-for-service base operating DRG payments for the fiscal year. The reduction is calculated from a rolling performance period and is capped at 3 percent (a 0.97 payment adjustment factor at most).

title: Pre- and post-discharge risk factors for hospital readmission among patients with diabetes
authors: Karunakaran A, Zhao H, Rubin DJ
passages: In a retrospective single-center study of hospitalized patients with diabetes, the lack of an outpatient follow-up visit within 30 days of discharge was the most striking predictor of readmission: patients without a follow-up visit had roughly 5.7 times the odds of readmission (OR 5.74, 95% CI 5.35-6.15).

A hospital discharge within the 90 days before the index admission was associated with 76% higher odds of readmission (OR 1.76, 95% CI 1.64-1.89), making recent prior utilization one of the strongest signals of near-term readmission risk.

Patients discharged against medical advice (AMA) had 60% higher odds of readmission than those discharged home (OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.32-1.94); having left AMA in the prior year was also linked to higher odds (OR 1.27).

An extreme blood glucose level during the index hospitalization (below 2.2 or above 16.6 mmol/L) was associated with 20% higher odds of readmission (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.10-1.31); pre-admission insulin use was associated with 14% higher odds (OR 1.14).

Longer length of stay was associated with higher readmission odds (OR 1.14 per log-unit increase). The overall 30-day readmission rate in this cohort was 20.4%; the authors note these are retrospective associations, not proof of causation.

title: Intensification of diabetes medication and risk for 30-day readmission
authors: Wei NJ, Wexler DJ, Nathan DM, Grant RW
passages: In a retrospective study of 1,949 adults with type 2 diabetes admitted to hospital between 2007 and 2009, about one in six patients (17%) had an early readmission or emergency department visit.

Across the full cohort, intensifying diabetes medication during hospitalization was not associated with early readmission (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.64-1.37) -- more aggressive inpatient glucose management did not, by itself, raise or lower short-term readmission risk.

Among patients with poor baseline glycemic control (HbA1c at or above 8%), medication intensification during hospitalization was associated with significantly lower early readmission risk (adjusted OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.12-0.88).

In that same poorly-controlled subgroup, post-discharge HbA1c fell by a mean of 1.8 percentage points in patients whose regimen was intensified, versus 0.6 points in those whose regimen was not -- intensification 'worked' pharmacologically and was not accompanied by more early returns to care.

title: Risk factors for 30-day readmission following hypoglycemia-related emergency room and inpatient admissions
authors: Emons MF, Bae JP, Hoogwerf BJ, et al.
passages: A broad diabetes population was found to have an all-cause 30-day ER-or-hospital readmission rate of 24.5%, higher than the 18.1% reported elsewhere for Medicare beneficiaries hospitalized specifically for hypoglycemia.
Insulin-related hypoglycemia accounted for an estimated 97,000 emergency department visits per year in the US (2007-2011); roughly one-third of those ED visits led to hospitalization.

Nearly half of readmitted patients had a recent hospitalization, or a stay in a skilled nursing facility, home health, or hospice, within the 90 days before the index visit -- recent prior utilization was strongly associated with readmission.

Young adults were at increased readmission risk even after adjusting for diabetes type and comorbidities; Medicaid-insured patients also had elevated adjusted risk, which the authors attribute in part to socioeconomic barriers to care access and coordination.

title: Predictors of 30-day unplanned hospital readmission among adult patients with diabetes mellitus: a systematic review with meta-analysis
authors: Soh JGS, Wong WP, Mukhopadhyay A, et al.
passages: A systematic review pooling 18 studies (covering 1 to 15 years of data collection, published 1998-2018) on 30-day unplanned readmission in adults with diabetes mellitus found heart failure (OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.67-1.96) and renal disease (OR 1.69, 95% CI 1.34-2.12) among the strongest comorbidity predictors.
Insulin therapy was associated with higher odds of readmission (OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.24-1.71) across the pooled studies.
Insurance/payer status was also a comparatively strong predictor of readmission (OR 1.41, 95% CI 1.22-1.63), on par with comorbidity burden and insulin use.

Age, gender, and race were identified as contributing factors, but were consistently weaker predictors than comorbidity burden, insulin therapy, and insurance status. The authors suggest targeting diabetes self-management education at patients defined by these stronger-predictor groups.

title: Predictors of frequency of 1-year readmission in adult patients with diabetes
authors: Soh JGS, Mukhopadhyay A, Mohankumar B, et al.
passages: A zero-inflated negative binomial model of 1-year readmission frequency in adults with diabetes identified renal disease (1.60x expected readmissions, 95% CI 1.34-1.92) and peripheral vascular disease (1.42x, 95% CI 1.07-1.90) as the two comorbidities most associated with repeat readmission.

Each additional emergency department visit in the prior period was associated with a 27% increase in expected readmissions (95% CI 1.15-1.41); each additional medication was associated with a 5% increase per drug (95% CI 1.03-1.07).
Each additional year of age was associated with roughly a 1% increase in expected readmissions (95% CI 1.001-1.012) -- a small but consistent per-year effect.
31.7% of patients had at least one readmission within a year of the index admission. The authors caution that the model should be validated in a prospective cohort before clinical adoption.

title: Patterns of engagement with the health care system and risk of subsequent hospitalization amongst patients with diabetes
authors: Ronksley PE, Ravani P, Sanmartin C, et al.
passages: In a cohort of 33,811 adults with diabetes, 32.8% had a subsequent all-cause hospitalization within a mean follow-up of 0.68 years; each emergency department visit in the prior year was associated with a 4% higher risk of subsequent hospitalization (adjusted HR 1.04, 95% CI 1.03-1.05).

Primary care utilization had a U-shaped relationship with risk: patients with 10 or more primary care visits in the prior year had higher subsequent-hospitalization risk than those with 1-4 visits (adjusted HR 1.23, 95% CI 1.16-1.29), and patients with zero primary care visits also trended toward higher risk, though this was significant only in a sensitivity analysis.

Patients who left a hospitalization against medical advice (AMA) had a 74% higher adjusted risk of subsequent hospitalization than those discharged home (adjusted HR 1.74, 95% CI 1.50-2.02); for diabetes-specific hospitalizations the adjusted HR rose to 2.86 (95% CI 1.82-4.49).
The authors describe their findings on care-engagement patterns as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive, given the observational design.
